title: Jason Arday was a victim of the worst kind of media pile-on
gist: Former Cambridge professor Jason Arday, exposed as a probable plagiarist, became a media symbol of 'woke' academic decline and died amid the coverage; the author, a former Oxford college head, shows Cambridge's actual black-professor numbers (5 out of roughly 1,250, or 0.4 per cent) contradict the DEI-bias narrative, and contrasts the pile-on against Arday with the far lighter scrutiny of Dr Nathan Cofnas, the self-declared 'racial realist' who broke the story and was himself dismissed by Cambridge for arguing black people are genetically less capable of academic merit.

insights.claim: To a certain breed of British journalist, the Jason Arday story — a black academic given a prestigious Cambridge professorship who turned out to be a probable plagiarist and 'fabulist' — was irresistible proof that 'wokery' was destroying elite universities, generating a sustained media pile-on before his death.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: States the article's core claim: Arday became a vehicle for a pre-existing media narrative about diversity policy rather than being covered on his own individual merits.
insights.quote: To a certain breed of British journalist, the Jason Arday story was irresistible catnip. He seemed to be the living, breathing proof that wokery was destroying our most august universities.
insights.locator: To a certain breed of British journalist

insights.claim: A Telegraph columnist called Arday 'a symptom of Labour's war on academic excellence,' even though his appointment actually took place under Rishi Sunak's government.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Illustrates a factual error in the media narrative — the appointment happened under a Conservative, not Labour, government — that went uncorrected in the coverage.
insights.quote: To one Telegraph columnist, he was “a symptom of Labour’s war on academic excellence” (though his questionable appointment happened under Rishi Sunak).

insights.claim: A Spectator column by Conservative peer Toby Young ran the headline calling the Arday story 'the gift that keeps giving.'
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence of the tone of glee in the coverage the author is criticising.
insights.quote: Arday was, as the headline on a Spectator column by Toby Young—a Conservative peer—sniggered, “the gift that keeps giving.”

themes.theme: Dr Nathan Cofnas: the story's source

insights.claim: Dr Nathan Cofnas, who claimed credit for unmasking Arday, shared a gleeful YouTube conversation with historian David Starkey, whose own Cambridge career ended six years earlier after he claimed slavery was not genocide because of the survival of 'so many damn blacks.'
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Identifies the source of the Arday allegations as someone with his own history of racially charged Cambridge controversy.
insights.quote: he shared an at times gleeful YouTube conversation with David Starkey, the TV historian whose own Cambridge career had come to a shuddering halt six years ago when he pronounced that slavery was not genocide because of the survival of “so many damn blacks”.
insights.locator: Among those apparently enjoying a good laugh

insights.claim: In the YouTube conversation, Starkey said 'the reason we are both grinning is that we are enjoying vengeance... Good, honest, straightforward, and Christian vengeance… we can rejoice together,' while Cofnas said 'Sophocles himself could not have come up with a more appropriate person to break this story than me.'
insights.speaker: David Starkey
insights.so_what: Direct quotes revealing the tone of personal vindication and vengeance driving the men who broke the story, undercutting any claim of dispassionate scrutiny.
insights.quote: “The reason we are both grinning is that we are enjoying vengeance,” chortled Starkey at the top of the programme. “Good. honest, straightforward, and Christian vengeance … we can rejoice together.”
insights.locator: It was a meeting of discarded souls

insights.claim: Cofnas himself had lost his own junior research fellowship at Emmanuel College, Cambridge, earlier this year after publishing a blog post arguing Harvard would have virtually no Black professors if appointments were made purely on merit.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Shows the story's central 'whistleblower' had his own recent, comparable controversy that received far less scrutiny than Arday's.
insights.quote: Cofnas related at some length how he had himself lost his role at Emmanuel College, Cambridge, earlier this year after publishing a long, rambling blog post in which he opined that Harvard would have virtually no Black professors if they were appointed purely on merit.

insights.claim: Cofnas wrote in February 2024 that 'in a meritocracy, Harvard faculty would be recruited from the best of the best students, which means the number of black professors would approach 0%,' and that without 'wokeism,' Black people 'would disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment.'
insights.speaker: Nathan Cofnas
insights.so_what: Documents the explicit racial-merit claims underlying Cofnas's worldview and his motivation in pursuing the Arday story.
insights.quote: In a meritocracy,” he wrote in February 2024, “Harvard faculty would be recruited from the best of the best students, which means the number of black professors would approach 0%.” He went further: without wokeism “[b]lacks would disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment.”
insights.locator: This was certainly Cofnas’s own take

insights.claim: In 2019, Cofnas published a paper in the journal Philosophical Psychology that was denounced by nine tenured professors, who compared his ideas to anti-vaxxers, creationists and climate change deniers, and said his article could reasonably be read as pandering to proponents of scientific racism.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Establishes that Cofnas's academic credibility was already formally challenged by peers years before the Arday story, unlike the media's uncritical use of him as a source.
insights.quote: it is undeniable that his article can reasonably be read as pandering to proponents of scientific racism. These strands of society obviously enjoy it when scholarly forums publish work that in some way legitimises their harmful ideas.

insights.claim: Unlike Arday, Cofnas's own Cambridge appointment and dismissal have not prompted calls for an independent inquiry into whether his hiring reveals disturbing truths about Cambridge's recruitment processes.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Highlights the asymmetric scrutiny applied to the two men's comparable Cambridge controversies.
insights.quote: there were no calls for an independent inquiry into whether the Cofnas appointment tells us disturbing truths about Cambridge’s hiring processes
insights.locator: But, anyway, it seems that no one cared

themes.theme: The data doesn't support the 'woke Cambridge' narrative

insights.claim: According to the Higher Education Statistics Agency, only 75 of Cambridge's 6,180 academics identified as black last year, and apart from Arday there were just five black professors, or 0.4 per cent of Cambridge's professorial rank.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Provides the key statistical counter-evidence to the narrative that Cambridge is 'awash' with DEI-driven black hires — the actual numbers are minimal.
insights.quote: Last year, just 75 of Cambridge’s 6,180 academics identified as black, according to the Higher Education Statistics Agency. Apart from Arday, there were just five black professors, or 0.4 per cent of Cambridge’s rank of professors.

insights.claim: Cambridge's latest five-year admissions figures show 542 places went to students identifying as black, about 4.6 per cent of admissions, while 27.5 per cent of places went to pupils from independent schools, which had a 21 per cent success rate compared with 15.5 per cent for comprehensive-school applicants.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Shows private-school applicants still substantially outperform state-school applicants in Cambridge admissions, undermining claims that the system is biased against traditional elites.
insights.quote: Last year 27.5 per cent of places went to pupils from independent schools. They had a success rate of 21 per cent compared with 15.5 per cent from comprehensives.
insights.locator: Nor does it appear that these supposedly

insights.claim: The author, drawing on the data, concludes that Cambridge could almost be described as the sort of university Cofnas himself would approve of — one employing virtually zero per cent black professors — meaning the institution is 'not very woke at all.'
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Directly rebuts the premise that drove the Arday coverage using Cofnas's own stated standard against him.
insights.quote: You could almost say that Cambridge is just the sort of university that Dr Cofnas admires: one which employs virtually zero per cent of black professors. So, not very woke at all.

insights.claim: The author's own experience as head of an Oxford college was that colleagues were extremely wary of anything that could be interpreted as 'lowering standards,' even while being willing to make modest allowances for an applicant's background.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Provides firsthand institutional testimony that elite university admissions culture is cautious rather than aggressively pro-diversity, contradicting the media narrative.
insights.quote: My own experience at the other place—as the head of an Oxford college—was that, while colleagues were keen to make modest changes to allow for the context of an applicant’s background, they were overall extremely wary of anything at all that could be interpreted as “lowering standards”.
insights.locator: My own experience at the other place

insights.claim: The author coined the term 'Marlborough Man' after a fellow college head described an irate letter in the Times from a parent protesting that his son, educated at Marlborough College (fees currently £64k a year), failed even to get an Oxford interview despite stellar exam grades.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Illustrates the specific social pressure — from wealthy, well-connected families — that shapes elite admissions caution, as a counterpoint to the DEI-bias narrative.
insights.quote: There was a particular paranoia about what one might call Marlborough Man—a name I coined after speaking to a fellow college head who had just read an irate letter in the Times protesting at the failure of his Marlborough College-educated son (fees currently £64k a year) even to get an interview at Oxford despite stellar exam grades.

insights.claim: A cautious college-head colleague told the author, 'You see, we have to tread carefully... It's only a matter of time before the system is judicially reviewed,' reflecting fear of legal challenge from wealthy families over admissions decisions.
insights.speaker: unnamed college head (quoted by Alan Rusbridger)
insights.so_what: Shows admissions officers' caution is driven partly by fear of litigation from well-resourced 'Marlborough Man' families, not by pro-diversity zeal.
insights.quote: “You see, we have to tread carefully,” said my cautious colleague. “It’s only a matter of time before the system is judicially reviewed. Its ability to behave sufficiently consistently across the piste will be exposed.”
insights.locator: You see, we have to tread carefully

insights.claim: The author argues an unspoken 'Marlborough factor' — anticipation of a litigious rejected applicant challenging the system — is also at work at Cambridge, with the expectation that Old Marlburians, not black or working-class white pupils, are the ones likely to claim discrimination.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Reframes the institutional risk calculus at elite universities as centred on wealthy-family litigation risk rather than DEI overreach.
insights.quote: The unspoken Marlborough factor will also be at work at Cambridge: the anticipation that a litigious rejectee (or his parents) might hold the system up to challenge on the grounds that Old Marlburians—and not black or working-class white pupils—are the ones being discriminated against.

insights.claim: The author acknowledges something clearly went wrong with Arday's appointment, and that multiple investigations have been launched into his claims, background and research, and into why Cambridge appointed and then defended him.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Balances the piece by not denying Arday's genuine misconduct, distinguishing the author's critique of the coverage from a defence of Arday's conduct itself.
insights.quote: Something clearly went badly wrong with the appointment of Arday. Multiple investigations have been launched into Arday’s claims, his background, his research—and into why Cambridge not only appointed him, but also defended him when doubts were raised.

insights.claim: The author's ultimate conclusion is that Arday's death should teach a lesson in not rushing to glib judgements, not joining the unthinking media pack, and keeping a sense of proportion and plain humanity.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: States the article's final normative takeaway about media conduct in cases involving race and academic scandal.
insights.quote: But maybe his death can offer us lessons in not rushing to glib judgements; in not joining the unthinking pack; and—above all—in keeping a sense of proportion and plain humanity.
insights.locator: But maybe his death can offer us lessons
